title: Seventy factories close in Savar and Ashulia as wage protests go on
excerpt: Border guards joined police on 5 November, and the NBR froze bank accounts of more than 100 people it links to the unrest.
content:
Seventy of the 1,863 factories in Savar and Ashulia, outside Dhaka, declared a holiday on Thursday, 5 November, as garment workers kept up protests for a Tk 30,000 monthly minimum wage, The Daily Star reported.

Clashes and arrests

At about 8:30am, protesters blocked the Abdullahpur-Baipail road at Jamgora. Police cleared it with tear gas and sound grenades after protesters threw bricks and stones and damaged a police vehicle, the newspaper reported. About an hour later, around 500 people broke two gates at Febrica Knit Composite in Dosaid, Ashulia, and the factory closed for security reasons.

Five platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) were deployed alongside police. Lt Col Taimur Hasan Khan, commander of 5 BGB, said the situation had improved and no disorder or sabotage had been reported. Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, described the situation as “fairly good”.

Mohammad Mostafizur Rahman, deputy inspector general of Dhaka Range, said 25 to 30 people had been arrested and eight cases filed. He said none of those arrested were workers and blamed a group trying to create anarchy. These figures come from police and have not been independently verified.

Khairul Mamun Mintu, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, condemned the arrests and cases and called for direct talks with workers, according to the report.

Bank accounts frozen

The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has frozen the bank accounts of more than 100 individuals and is examining transactions of about 125 companies, The Daily Star reported on the same day, citing NBR sources. The stated aim is to trace whether money was used to fund the unrest.

The NBR’s Central Intelligence Cell and the Income Tax Intelligence and Investigation Unit asked banks to freeze the accounts and share the companies’ records, the report said. Most of the individuals are linked to the ousted Awami League government, including former ministers, lawmakers and business owners. Those named include Salman F Rahman of Beximco Group, Tipu Munshi and SM Mannan Kochi, a former president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA).

“We are working according to our higher authorities’ directions,” a senior NBR official told the newspaper, speaking on condition of anonymity. The government alleges that politically connected people helped start and fund the unrest.

Why it matters

The dispute is now a security and political matter as well as a wage question. NGOs and labour rights groups running programmes with garment workers in Savar and Ashulia should expect continued disruption and should take care with staff safety around protest sites. The Minimum Wage Board has agreed that new wages will start in December, but has not yet set an amount.

What to watch

Whether factories reopen on Saturday, when the wage board meets next, and whether the account freezes lead to formal cases.
